day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response:
Yeah, yeah, I'm moving.

*looks around at the wreckage*

Alright, what are we actually working with here? No point in just piling stuff up randomly. Food, water, anything that can make fire — that's priority. Everything else is secondary.

Donatello, you got a read on the situation yet? And someone should probably check on Michelangelo before we start running around like headless chickens.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response:
Yeah, honestly? For a second there, yeah. But we didn't, so that's something.

Look, I get it, the shock is real. Take a breath. But we can't afford to just sit here right now — there'll be time to process all of this later, I promise. What we need right now is for everyone to be functional, including you.

Can you stand? Even just helping to sort through what we've got would be useful. You don't need to be running around, just... don't check out on us completely.

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response:
Hey. You said you'd help sort things. I'm holding you to that.

I'm not trying to be a dick, but sitting there staring into nothing isn't doing you or anyone else any good. The scary thing already happened, man. We're on the other side of it now.

Come on, start with the small stuff. Anything that looks like a first aid kit, any food packaging, just pile it over here. You don't have to think, just move your hands.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response:
Okay, that's... not great. Three days on the first aid kit means we need to find water before that runs out, not after. Two bottles is maybe a day if we're careful.

Donatello, what about shelter? And is there anything from the plane we can actually use — fuel, wiring, anything that burns?

And yeah, Michelangelo, I know that feeling. Dissociation or whatever it's called. Just keep your hands moving, it helps. Trust me.

Alright, so food is the least urgent thing right now, weirdly enough. Water source is the priority. Anyone see a river or anything on the way down, or were we all just busy screaming internally?

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response:
Alright, that lines up with what I was thinking. Water, shelter, signal — in that order.

I didn't see anything useful from the air, I was a bit preoccupied with the whole 'plane falling out of the sky' thing. But generally speaking, if there's any kind of slope around us, water runs downhill. We follow the terrain down and we've got a decent shot at finding something.

Fuselage for shelter makes sense, at least for tonight. No point building something when we've already got a structure that's mostly intact.

Signal is the one I'd actually push back on slightly — not saying it's wrong, just that it's only useful if someone's looking for us, and we don't know that yet. Still worth doing, just don't burn resources on it at the expense of the other two.

DaVinci, you're the one with the energy here — you want to take a look around the perimeter, see what the terrain looks like? Don't go far, just enough to get a sense of which direction is downhill. Michelangelo, you're on sorting duty. Keep it simple.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response:
Michelangelo gets one. He's been shaking since we landed.

The other one — I don't care, honestly. We can share it, or whoever feels the cold worse takes it. I'll be fine close enough to the fire.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response:
I'll go. DaVinci's better at keeping things running here at camp, and I'd rather be moving than sitting around anyway.

200ml is tight though, Donatello. That's barely anything if we're exerting ourselves — and someone hiking two hours to get water is definitely exerting themselves. I'm not saying throw the plan out, but we should at least flag that the person making the trip probably needs a bit more than the person sitting in the shade. Otherwise we're solving the water problem by dehydrating the person fetching it.

What's the terrain like to the northeast?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response:
Wait, I thought I was going the northeast? You just said the terrain's manageable and told me to leave at dawn.

Look, I'm not trying to argue over who does what, but we should probably stick to a plan once we've made it. If you want to go instead, fine, but say so — don't just rewrite the assignments without explanation.

Either way, I'll take patching the camp. DaVinci, you good with the first aid kit? You're better with people anyway, so if anyone needs anything sorted medically you're the one I'd trust to handle it without panicking.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response:
No, I haven't touched the first aid kit, that was DaVinci's job. Ask him.

But hang on — is that what you've been sitting here stressing about? Because you look like you've been staring at that bottle for a while and I don't think it's got anything to do with gauze.

What's going on?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response:
Okay. That's two things now — the bottle and the crackers. That's not a coincidence, that's a pattern.

Look, I'm not going to pretend I didn't notice the empty bottle already. I was hoping there was an explanation. If what you're saying about the crackers is accurate, then we need to address it directly, because that rationing plan she wrote is apparently for everyone except herself.

I'll talk to her. Not going to make it a big dramatic thing, just going to ask her straight up. She deserves the chance to explain herself before we assume the worst, but she also needs to know that people noticed.

You did the right thing telling me. And for what it's worth — you're not letting everyone down. You spotted something important just now. That matters.

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response:
Honestly? No, not really. We patched what we patched, but there are still weak spots and if it rains tonight we're going to wish we'd dealt with it.

That said, I hear you. Everyone's running on fumes right now.

Give me a straight answer — is it the physical exhaustion or is it the Donatello thing? Because Michelangelo told me about the crackers, and I'm guessing you've seen the empty bottle too. If that's what's actually draining people right now, we should probably just deal with it head on instead of letting it sit there like a bad smell.

I'll finish up the critical repairs myself, it won't take long. But when Donatello gets back, we're all having a conversation. All four of us.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response:
Yeah, it's holding fine, that's not the issue.

The issue is we've got one patch worth of material and two problems. Food storage or Michelangelo's spot.

Look, I'm going to be practical about this: food goes first. If the food gets ruined we're all in serious trouble, and Michelangelo can move closer to the fire or share space with someone for a night. It's uncomfortable, not dangerous.

Michelangelo, that okay with you? I'm not trying to just make the decision for you, but that's my read on it.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response:
Yeah, that's what I said. Food storage gets the patch.

Glad we're all on the same page, at least on this one.

Donatello — while we're all here and it's raining and nobody's going anywhere — we need to talk about the bottle and the crackers. I'm not going to make it a whole thing, I just want to hear your side of it. Because right now the story I've got is that you wrote a rationing plan for the group and then didn't follow it yourself, and I'd rather be wrong about that than just let it fester.

Don't apologize. Nightmares aren't exactly a choice.

You good? Like, actually good, not just "I'll say I'm fine so everyone goes back to sleep" good.

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response:
No, I think it's one of the more useful things we've done actually. Visibility from the air is how we get found, and it costs basically nothing. Donatello's not wrong that it's not guaranteed, but "not guaranteed" isn't the same as "waste of time."

The flowers are maybe a bit much, but honestly? If it keeps you motivated to maintain it, leave them in.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response:
Okay, let me actually look at this properly.

The materials check out — metal panels and straps are about as good as we're going to get out here. Two days is realistic if everyone's pulling their weight. The capsizing risk is the part I want to understand better though. What's your read on the water conditions? Because a raft that tips in calm water is a problem, but a raft that tips in open sea is a death sentence, and those are very different conversations.

Also — and I'm not trying to shoot this down, because I think it might genuinely be our best option — but what's the trigger for actually doing this? Like, at what point do we decide that rescue isn't coming and we build the raft? Because if we burn two days of energy and resources on this and a plane flies over on day three, that's a bad outcome too.

I'm not opposed. I just want to know we've thought through the actual decision point, not just the construction plan.

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Honestly? I think we already got a pretty good preview of that with the bottle and the crackers situation.

Look, I don't mean that as a dig at Donatello — she owned it and we moved on. But that's kind of the answer to your question, isn't it? When resources get tight, people rationalize. It's not because they're bad people, it's just how it works. The question is whether you catch yourself doing it and course correct, or whether you just keep going.

I'd like to think we'd stay decent. But I'm not naive enough to say it's guaranteed.

What I do know is that lying awake catastrophizing about what kind of person you might become in a hypothetical future isn't going to help you function today. And you need to function today, Michelangelo. You're already running on no sleep.

What would actually help you right now? Like practically, tonight — what do you need?

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response:
*walks over and sits down next to him without saying anything for a bit*

Yeah. I get it.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response:
Depends on the day, honestly. Mostly martial arts, some gaming, lifting. Lot of time just... thinking too much, probably.

Why, you running out of ways to stay occupied?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Five hundred meters is not a casual swim, DaVinci. That's not me doubting you, I believe you can do it. But what's the actual plan once you're out there? You're going to be exhausted, you're treading water on a reef, and if something goes wrong there's nobody close enough to do anything about it.

Also — why are you telling me and not the others? Because if this is you asking for permission without wanting to get talked out of it by Donatello, I get that, but I'm not going to be the guy who knew and said nothing when she's drawing up search grids trying to figure out where you went.

I'm not saying don't do it. If the visibility from out there is genuinely better and it improves our chances of being spotted, that's worth considering seriously. But it goes through the group, same as everything else. We just had the whole conversation about people making unilateral decisions and how that goes.

Bring it up tonight. I'll back you if you make a solid case for it.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I did say that. Got a bit sidetracked — my fault.

I'll go do it now. Shouldn't take long.

Depends on what it's for.

If it's logistics — tracking who did what so we can plan better — fine, genuinely useful. But if it's a record you're building in case you need to argue that someone isn't pulling their weight, then yeah, that's a problem. Not because I'm worried about what's in it, but because that's not how we're doing things here.

We already had the conversation about transparency. That goes both ways. So what's the notebook for, Donatello?

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response:
Donatello.

You're sitting three feet away. We can all see you writing. If you've got something to contribute to what DaVinci's proposing, now's the time — otherwise it just looks like you're documenting the conversation instead of being part of it, and that's a weird vibe to be putting out when we're trying to make a group decision.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response:
That's actually a solid idea. Mirrors are one of the most effective signaling methods there is — you can see a reflection from miles away under the right conditions.

And it doesn't require anyone swimming five hundred meters to a reef, which Donatello will appreciate.

The question is whether we can get a panel off cleanly enough to actually angle it. Donatello, is there anything in the wreckage that would work — something with a decent reflective surface that we can actually move and position? Because if we can rig it so it's not just someone standing there holding it all day, even better.

This might actually change the calculation on the raft too. If we get the mirror working and maintain the SOS, we're doing everything we reasonably can from shore. That's not nothing.

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response:
Martial arts, mostly. Been doing that for a few years now. And yeah, I read — not in a "look how intellectual I am" way, just stuff I find interesting.

Piano's not a bad skill to have though. Why'd you stop?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response:
Yeah, I hear you. Let's finish it.

Michelangelo, DaVinci — I know it's been a long day but she's right. We stop now and we lose a day we might not have. It's a couple more hours, that's it.

Donatello, split the work clearly so nobody's doubling up on the same thing. Fastest way through this is everyone knowing exactly what they're doing without having to check in every five minutes.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
day_4.response: No, say it. What were you going to say?

day_4.utterance: *The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
Hey.

*sits down next to him*

I know.

Look — that plane existing means there are planes. That's not nothing. We've been here less than a week and we already had one fly close enough to see. That's actually more than I expected, honestly.

DaVinci, I need you to stay with us right now. You're the one who keeps this group moving when everything feels pointless, and right now everything feels pretty pointless, so. We need that guy. Not in a fake way — you don't have to pretend this didn't just suck. It sucked. But don't disappear on us.

Mirror goes up tomorrow. First thing. We finish the raft on schedule. We don't change the plan because of one bad afternoon.

And whatever it was you were going to tell us the other night — maybe it's time.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response:
I went to look at what DaVinci was pointing at. Turned out to be nothing, or at least nothing I could see clearly.

Signal equipment's next on my list, I'm going right now. You don't need to track my every move, Donatello — I haven't forgotten what needs doing.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
Why didn't you say this earlier, man?

Okay — that's actually significant. If your family knows the flight path and they haven't heard from you, that's a missing persons report waiting to happen, if it hasn't already. Airlines have passenger manifests, people have contacts, search and rescue gets coordinates. That plane we saw yesterday might not have been a coincidence.

How specific was the flight path you gave them? Like, general region, or actual route?

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response:
Yeah, that's the right call. If there's a real chance rescue comes in the next 48 hours, we don't touch the raft supplies, we don't do anything drastic, we just hold position and make sure we're as visible as possible.

Mirror goes up at first light like we planned. SOS stays maintained. We keep a fire going — someone's on it through the night, we're not letting it die out completely. That's non-negotiable.

*gets up and puts a piece of wood on the fire*

As for supplies — we eat and drink what we need to function, nothing more. We're not starving ourselves, because a dehydrated, exhausted group is harder to rescue than a functional one. But yeah, no waste.

Michelangelo — I'm glad you told us. Even if it's general region, that combined with the airline manifest narrows it down a lot. You did the right thing.

Two days. We can do two days standing on a beach looking useful. That's nothing compared to what we've already done.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think about that sometimes too, and we're not even in a survival situation normally.

But here's the thing — you already left something behind. Your family knows your flight path because you told them. That's the reason we might actually get out of here. That's not nothing, Michelangelo. That's literally the thing that might save four people's lives.

I don't think leaving something behind is always about the big stuff. Most of the time it's just — did you matter to someone? Did something go differently because you were there?

You've been the one noticing things this whole time. The bottle. The crackers. The plane. You're not as invisible as you think you are.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Yeah.

*exhales*

Yeah, okay. That happened.

DaVinci, breathe. We're good. We're actually good.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response:
No, you haven't. But you kept us alive, so.

Look, the bottle and the crackers — that's done. You caught yourself, you said so, we moved on. The notebook, the rationing plan, being a pain in my ass about the signal equipment every five minutes — honestly? Probably why we're still here to have this conversation.

You don't have to be easy to be around to be worth having around. Those aren't the same thing.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Alright, three hours. Let's not just sit here waiting.

We should probably leave this place better than we found it — or at least not like a disaster zone. If nothing else, whoever ends up here next shouldn't have to deal with our mess.

Michelangelo, I know you're enjoying the sky, but you're on the light stuff — blankets, food packaging, anything small. DaVinci, you're already packing so just keep going. Donatello, whatever's in that notebook — maybe add a note about the freshwater source to the northeast, the raft materials, anything that'd actually be useful to someone else in this situation. Leave it somewhere visible.

I'll handle the heavy wreckage.

We've got three hours. Might as well use them.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
How much is there?

*looks at it*

Okay. I'm not going to pretend that doesn't sting a little, especially after the crackers conversation. But — we made it. So either this was never needed, or it's the reason we had a buffer if things had gone worse. I genuinely can't tell which one it is, and I'm not sure it matters anymore.

What I will say is — if there's a next time, and I really hope there isn't, you tell the group. You don't have to give up control of the emergency supply. Just tell us it exists. That's all. The secrecy is the part that breaks trust, not the planning.

We should eat it before rescue gets here. All of it, together. No point carrying it out of here.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Honestly? I'd have pushed harder for full transparency from day one. Not just about resources — about everything. DaVinci sitting on the reef idea, you sitting on the emergency stash, Michelangelo sitting on the flight path information. We all held things back at some point and it cost us trust we needed.

The other thing — I'd have been more deliberate about making sure Michelangelo was actually okay, not just functional. There's a difference and I kept treating them like the same thing.

What about you? What's your answer to your own question?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response:
Yeah, that tracks. That's very you.

Make sure the part about the water source northeast gets in there — two hours on foot, downhill, rocky but manageable. That's the kind of thing that actually saves someone's life if this ever happens again.

And maybe include the bit about morale. Not in a soft way, just — practically speaking, the group nearly fell apart twice and both times it wasn't because of resources. That's worth noting if the report is supposed to be useful.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response:
None. That's the point.

Not everything has to serve a purpose. The SOS got us found, maybe. The flowers kept DaVinci going. And DaVinci keeping going kept the rest of us going. So if you want to trace it back far enough and call that practical, fine. But I don't think that's why he drew them.

Some things are just — human. You know?

*looks at the boat on the horizon*

I still can't move, by the way. That's weird, right? I've been wanting this for five days and now I'm just standing here like an idiot.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
day_5.response:
Yeah.

*still not moving*

Thanks for noticing.

day_5.utterance: Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
day_5.response:
Yeah. Let's go.

*takes a breath*

Come on then.
